faq.question: How do you mix 10 and 30 volume developer to make 20 volume?
faq.answer: To formulate 20 Volume (6%) developer, mix equal parts (1:1 ratio) of 10 Volume (3%) and 30 Volume (9%) developer. For example, 30ml of 10 Vol + 30ml of 30 Vol equals 60ml of 20 Vol developer.

faq.question: Can I mix different developer brands together?
faq.answer: No. Different manufacturers formulate developers with proprietary buffers, conditioning agents, and viscosity stabilizers. Blending different brands can cause emulsion breakdown or unpredictable lift.

faq.question: Can you dilute 40 volume developer with water to make 20 volume?
faq.answer: Never use water to dilute developer. Water dilutes the preservative system, alters the pH balance, and thins the product consistency, causing bleeding into foils or scalp irritation.

faq.question: How does the Alligation calculation formula work?
faq.answer: The formula uses Pearson's Square (Alligation Alternate): Parts Low = High Vol - Target Vol; Parts High = Target Vol - Low Vol. Total parts equal Parts Low + Parts High.

education.heading: The Chemistry of Developer Volume Blending (The Alligation Method)
intro: Behind the chair, hydrogen peroxide (H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>) developers are the chemical oxidative drivers of permanent hair color, high-lift blonding, and toner deposit. The "Volume" rating denotes the volume of pure oxygen gas liberated from one volume of liquid developer during complete oxidation (for example, 20 Volume developer releases 20 times its volume in oxygen, representing approximately 6% hydrogen peroxide concentration by weight).

When a colorist runs out of 20 Volume mid-service, canceling appointments or estimating measurements compromises both lift and tonal deposit. Using the pharmaceutical Alligation Alternate method (the rule of mixtures), any two known developer concentrations from the same product line can be mathematically proportioned to create an exact intermediate strength without chemical guesswork.

walkthrough.title: The Exact Alligation Formula Walkthrough
steps: Step 1: Parts of Low Volume Needed = High Volume − Target Volume
Step 2: Parts of High Volume Needed = Target Volume − Low Volume
Step 3: Total Parts = Parts Low + Parts High
walkthrough.example:
Worked Example: Formulate 60ml of 20 Vol using 10 Vol and 30 Vol:
• Parts of 10 Vol = 30 − 20 = 10 parts
• Parts of 30 Vol = 20 − 10 = 10 parts
• Total Parts = 20 parts → Ratio is 10:10 (1:1 equal parts) → 30ml of 10 Vol + 30ml of 30 Vol = 60ml of 20 Vol.

education.rules_heading: Critical Station Rules for Mixing Developers

rules.title: Stay Within the Same Brand & Product Line
rules.body: Never cross-mix developers from different manufacturers (e.g. Wella with Redken). Manufacturers formulate with distinct lipid carriers, viscosity thickeners, and proprietary buffering agents that can destabilize when combined.

rules.title: Measure by Digital Weight (Grams or Ounces)
rules.body: Measuring by eyeball or cup lines introduces 10%–20% volumetric error. Always tare your mixing bowl on a 0.1g digital scale for exact formulation repeatability.

rules.title: Never Dilute Developer with Tap Water
rules.body: Adding tap water dilutes the preservative system, alters the pH balance, and causes emulsion thinning, leading to packet bleed and patchy lift. Always blend with a lower volume developer.

education.heading: Why Weighing Bleach and Developer Is Non-Negotiable
intro: In chemical lightening, potassium persulfate and ammonium persulfate salts require exact stoichiometry with hydrogen peroxide developer to lift melanin without compromising the structural keratin disulfide bonds.

Eyeballing lightener ratios or using volumetric plastic scoops introduces up to 30% inconsistency in chemical pH and viscosity. Too dry (under-ratio) and the persulfate crystals swell rapidly, crust over, and stop lifting. Too wet (over-ratio in foils) and developer peroxide dilutes the active persulfate concentration, causing packet slippage and chemical banding.

walkthrough.title: How to use this calculator
steps: Weigh your powder lightener on a tared digital scale and enter the gram (or ounce) amount.
Select the mixing ratio for the technique you are performing — thicker for open-air work, thinner for foils or a bleach bath.
Pour developer into the same bowl, on the same scale, until the total reaches the calculated bowl weight.
walkthrough.example: Example: 30g of powder at a 1:2 ratio needs 60g of developer, for a 90g total bowl weight.

name: Hair Level & Undertone Neutralizer Guide
description: Identify exposed warmth at levels 1 through 10 and look up the exact counteracting toner pigments on the color wheel.
intro: Every level of lift exposes a predictable underlying pigment—from red at Level 2 up to pale yellow at Level 9. Use this interactive chart to instantly identify the exact complementary pigment required to neutralize brassiness or enhance golden tones.
formula_summary: Color Wheel Rule: Green neutralizes Red (Levels 1–3), Blue neutralizes Orange (Levels 5–6), Violet neutralizes Yellow (Levels 8–10).
calc_subtitle: Drag the slider to the exposed lift level and instantly see the neutralizing pigment to use.

education.heading: Understanding the Color Wheel Rule
intro: Every time hair is lightened, it passes through a predictable sequence of underlying pigments — warm red at the darkest levels, through orange, into yellow and pale yellow at the lightest levels. This is the "exposed pigment" you are working against whenever you tone.

To neutralize an unwanted warm tone, you apply the complementary (opposite) color from the color wheel. The chart below maps each of the ten standard levels of lift to its exposed pigment and the complementary toner family that cancels it out.

walkthrough.title: How to read the chart
steps: Identify the level of lift you have reached (or are aiming for) after lightening — Level 1 is black, Level 10 is the lightest pale yellow/white.
Find that level's exposed undertone in the table — this is the warmth you will see in the hair.
Select a toner or color containing the matching neutralizer pigment shown alongside it.
Apply with a low-volume developer (typically 5–10 Vol) for a short processing time, since you are depositing tone rather than lifting further.
walkthrough.example: Example: hair has lifted to Level 7 and shows yellow-orange/gold-copper warmth. The color wheel calls for a blue-violet ash neutralizer — a toner in the .12 / .21 family — to cancel it.

rules.title: Green neutralizes Red
rules.body: Used at the darkest levels of lift (1–3), where the strongest warm/red pigment is exposed.

rules.title: Blue neutralizes Orange
rules.body: Used at mid-range levels of lift (5–6), as the exposed pigment shifts from red toward orange.

rules.title: Violet neutralizes Yellow
rules.body: Used at the lightest levels of lift (8–10), where the exposed pigment is yellow or pale yellow.

warnings: This chart is a formulation guide, not a guarantee — actual exposed warmth varies with hair porosity, prior chemical history, and the brand/line of color used.
Always perform a strand test before full application, especially on previously colored or chemically treated hair.
Follow your toner manufacturer's own developer volume and processing time directions — they take priority over the general guidance given here.
safety.manufacturer_note: Formulas use universal metric and imperial units compatible with major professional brands including Wella, Redken, Schwarzkopf, L'Oréal, and Guy Tang Mydentity, but exact pigment names and numbering vary by line — always cross-reference your own color system.

name: Grey Hair Coverage Formulation Calculator
description: Formulate exact base-to-fashion shade ratios based on client grey percentage (25%, 50%, 75%, 100%).
intro: Translucent grey hair lacks natural background pigment. To achieve 100% opaque coverage on stubborn grey hair, you must blend a dedicated Natural/Base series with your client's target fashion shade. This calculator provides the exact gram breakdown.
formula_summary: Standard Formulation: 25% grey = 25% Natural Base | 50% grey = 50% Natural Base | 75%+ grey = 66%–75% Natural Base with 20 Vol developer.
calc_subtitle: Enter grey percentage and batch size for the exact base-to-fashion shade gram breakdown.

education.heading: Why Grey Hair Needs a Base-to-Fashion Blend
intro: Grey hair has little to no natural background pigment — it is translucent, not simply "faded" like regrown natural hair. A fashion or demi-permanent shade applied alone on resistant grey will often look sheer, cool, or ashy because there is no underlying warmth for it to deposit onto.

A dedicated Natural/Base (N) series restores that missing background pigment, giving the fashion shade something to sit on top of. The more grey present, the more base is needed relative to the fashion shade.

walkthrough.title: How to use this calculator
steps: Estimate the client's grey percentage by sectioning the hair and visually assessing coverage.
Enter your total color batch size (the full amount you plan to mix).
Use the resulting Base (N) and Fashion Shade gram split to build your formula in the bowl.
Process with 20 Volume developer at a 1:1 or 1:1.5 ratio for a full 45 minutes on resistant cuticles.
walkthrough.example: Example: 50% grey hair with a 60g total batch needs 30g Natural Base (N) + 30g Fashion Shade.

rules.title: More grey means more base, not more developer
rules.body: Resistant grey needs more Natural Base pigment in the mix, not a higher developer volume — overprocessing with excess peroxide does not improve coverage and risks damage.

rules.title: Full processing time matters on resistant cuticles
rules.body: Grey hair's compact cuticle structure resists pigment deposit — cutting the 45-minute process short is the most common cause of grey "bleed-through" after a few washes.

warnings: Always perform a 48-hour client skin allergy patch test before chemical color services.
Follow your color manufacturer's own base/fashion blending ratios and developer volume guidance — they take priority over the general guidance given here.
safety.manufacturer_note: Base ratio percentages are a universal starting formula compatible with major professional brands including Wella, Redken, Schwarzkopf, L'Oréal, and Guy Tang Mydentity, but exact Natural/Base series naming and strength vary by line — always cross-reference your own color system.

faq.a: Enter the client's grey percentage and your total batch size. The calculator instantly gives you the Natural Base and Fashion Shade gram split — no page reloads.

faq.q: Are these measurements calibrated for all professional salon brands?
faq.a: The base ratio percentages are a universal starting point compatible with major brands including Wella, Redken, Schwarzkopf, L'Oréal, and Guy Tang Mydentity — always confirm your own line's recommended Natural/Base series and ratio range.

faq.q: Why does more grey need more base color instead of a stronger developer?
faq.a: Grey hair lacks background pigment, not porosity. A higher developer volume lifts hair but does not add missing pigment back in — only a Natural Base shade restores the warmth a fashion color needs to sit on top of.

education.heading: Why Balayage Pricing Needs Real Math, Not a Flat Rate
intro: Balayage is one of the highest-ticket services in the salon, but it is also one of the easiest to under-price. A flat "balayage starts at $X" rate ignores the fact that a long, thick head of hair can burn through two or three extra bowls of lightener and toner compared to a short, fine one — and every extra bowl is real backbar cost coming straight out of your margin.
Quoting from actual product usage and your target hourly rate, rather than a guess, is what protects your profit on the services that take the longest and look the most impressive on social media.

walkthrough.title: How to use this calculator
steps: Count how many bowls of lightener/clay the service will realistically need based on hair length and density.
Enter your actual product cost per bowl (check your backbar invoice, not a guess).
Add glosser/toner bowls and whether a bond builder like Olaplex or K18 is included.
Enter the total appointment time and your target net hourly labor rate.
The calculator adds backbar product cost to labor cost for a recommended quote and shows your approximate profit margin.
walkthrough.example: Example: 3 lightener bowls at $8.50, 2 toner bowls, a bond builder, 3.5 hours of labor at a $65/hour target rate recommends a $255 quote with roughly 86% going to labor margin.

rules.title: Price the appointment you actually did, not the one you planned
rules.body: If a service ran long or needed an extra bowl, that cost belongs in the quote or in next time's deposit/pricing conversation — not absorbed silently into your margin.

rules.title: Backbar cost compounds fast on long hair
rules.body: Extra bowls of lightener and toner are the single biggest margin killer on balayage — track real bowl counts per length category so your pricing reflects reality.

warnings: This tool estimates pricing only — it does not replace your own profit-and-loss tracking or accountant's advice on margins and tax.

education.heading: Damp vs Dry Toning: Why the Ratio and Timing Both Matter
intro: Toning damp, freshly lightened hair gives sheer, translucent results because the cuticle is still slightly raised and porous from the lightening service — the toner deposits lightly and blends. Toning dry hair, by contrast, allows for maximum pigment deposit, depth, and longevity, since the cuticle has fully closed.
The developer ratio controls dilution and lift intensity: a 1:1 ratio gives a standard, fuller-strength demi-permanent result, while a 1:2 ratio dilutes the toner for a sheerer, more subtle gloss.

walkthrough.title: How to use this calculator
steps: Measure your toner color amount.
Choose your developer ratio — 1:1 for standard depth, 1:2 for a sheer, diluted gloss.
Mix with 5–10 Volume dedicated toner developer.
Visual-check at 5 and 10 minutes for a standard demi, or every 5 minutes up to 15–20 minutes for a sheer gloss on damp hair.
walkthrough.example: Example: 30ml of toner at a 1:1 ratio needs 30ml of developer for a 60ml total mix.

rules.title: Damp hair tones lighter and sheerer
rules.body: The still-open cuticle from lightening means less pigment uptake — expect a softer result than the same formula on dry hair.

rules.title: Always visual-check, never process blind
rules.body: Toner can grab faster than expected on porous or over-processed hair — checking at regular intervals prevents overshooting the target shade.

warnings: Always perform a 48-hour client skin allergy patch test before chemical toning services.
Use only a dedicated toner/gloss developer at the volume your manufacturer specifies — mixing with a standard permanent-color developer can cause unpredictable results.
safety.manufacturer_note: Ratio math is a universal starting point compatible with major demi-permanent lines including Redken Shades EQ, Wella Color Touch, and Schwarzkopf Igora Vibrance, but exact developer volume and timing vary by line — always cross-reference your own manufacturer's instructions.

education.heading: Why Flat-Rate Color Correction Pricing Loses Money
intro: Color correction is inherently unpredictable — you cannot know exactly how many stages (decap, fill, foil, gloss) a head of hair will need until you are in it. Charging a single flat "color correction" rate regardless of complexity is one of the most common ways stylists end up working for below minimum wage on these appointments.
Breaking the service into discrete stages, each billed at a real hourly rate plus a backbar buffer, keeps the quote honest whether the correction takes two stages or six.

walkthrough.title: How to use this calculator
steps: Estimate the number of correction stages needed (e.g. color remover, fill, lightening, toning/gloss).
Enter your target hourly rate.
The calculator allocates 1.25 hours per stage and adds a $25/stage backbar buffer for the extra product correction work consumes.
walkthrough.example: Example: a 3-stage correction at an $85/hour target rate recommends a quote of roughly $394, covering about 3.75 hours of labor plus a $75 backbar buffer.

rules.title: Always quote a range before you start, then confirm once you see the hair
rules.body: Give the client an estimated stage range up front, and confirm the final quote once you have assessed porosity and prior chemical history in person.

rules.title: Backbar cost scales with stages, not just time
rules.body: Each additional stage consumes real product — a flat backbar assumption per stage keeps the quote honest even if labor time runs efficiently.

warnings: Color correction often involves multiple chemical services in one sitting — always assess hair integrity and consider splitting into multiple appointments if the hair cannot safely tolerate it in one visit.
This tool estimates pricing only — it does not replace your own professional judgment on what the hair can safely withstand.

intro: Foil count drives both product usage and appointment length. Underestimating foils mid-service means stopping to prep more sheets with lightener already activated in the bowl — a rushed, messy interruption. Overestimating wastes pre-cut sheets and backbar product.
Estimating the right range before you start lets you prep foils, mix the right batch size, and set an accurate appointment time with the client up front.

name: Perm Rod Size & Curl Diameter Guide
description: Determine perm rod diameter (red, yellow, blue, white, purple) to match client target wave or curl pattern.
intro: Perm rod selection determines the final curl diameter. Matching the rod size to the desired curl pattern (tight spiral vs beach wave) ensures optimal disulfide bond reformation without frizzy over-processing.
formula_summary: Rod Color Chart: Red (4mm tight), Yellow (5mm), Blue (9mm standard), White (11mm full wave), Purple (14mm beach wave).

education.heading: Matching Rod Size to Wave Pattern
intro: Perm rod diameter directly determines final curl size — smaller rods create tighter spirals, larger rods create soft, loose waves. Processing time also varies by rod size and hair porosity, so a one-size-fits-all timer risks over- or under-processing.
Choosing the right rod size and timing range up front, then confirming with a test curl, keeps the result predictable.

walkthrough.title: How to use this guide

rules.title: Always test curl before neutralizing
rules.body: A test curl confirms the perm has actually taken before you commit to neutralizing — skipping it risks an under-processed result that relaxes within days.

rules.title: Fine hair processes faster

calc_subtitle: Select hair length & density for the right keratin dosage and flat iron guidance.

education.heading: Dosing Keratin by Hair Length and Density
intro: Keratin smoothing treatments need enough product to coat every strand evenly without oversaturating — too little leaves patchy results, too much can cause buildup and a greasy, weighed-down finish that doesn't smooth properly under the flat iron.
Hair length and density are the two biggest drivers of how much product a head actually needs, along with how many flat iron passes are required to properly seal it in.

walkthrough.title: How to use this guide
steps: Select the client's hair length and density category.
Apply thin, even layers from mid-lengths to ends first, then roots last.
Flat iron with the number of passes and temperature range shown, then follow your brand's specific wash-wait time before the client showers.
walkthrough.example: Example: medium/normal hair typically needs 45–60ml of product and 4–6 flat iron passes at 400–430°F (204–221°C).

rules.title: Apply mid-lengths to ends first, roots last
rules.body: This sequencing avoids over-depositing product at the scalp where it is least needed and most likely to cause buildup or irritation.

rules.title: Follow brand-specific wash-wait time exactly
rules.body: Washing too soon after a keratin treatment can undo the bond before it has fully set, regardless of how well the application and flat ironing were done.

warnings: Many keratin smoothing treatments release formaldehyde or formaldehyde-releasing agents when heat-sealed — always ensure adequate salon ventilation and check your product's safety data sheet.
Always perform a 48-hour client skin allergy patch test before keratin smoothing services.
safety.manufacturer_note: Dosage ranges are a general guide — always follow your specific keratin brand's application amount, flat iron temperature, and wash-wait time instructions, as formulations vary significantly between brands.

faq.q: How much keratin product do I need for long, dense hair?
faq.a: Long or dense hair typically needs 75–90ml of product and 6–8 flat iron passes at 420–450°F (216–232°C).

faq.q: How do I use this calculator behind the chair?
faq.a: Select the client's hair length and density, and the guide instantly gives you a dosage range, iron pass count, and temperature guidance.

faq.q: Why does keratin need flat ironing at a specific temperature?
faq.a: The flat iron heat is what seals the keratin treatment into the hair shaft — too low a temperature won't properly bond it, while too high risks heat damage.
